Encounter.description: Represents a patient encounter or visit.

Condition.title: Condition
Condition.description: Represents a patient's medical condition or diagnosis.

Measurement.title: Measurement
Measurement.description: Represents a vital sign or lab measurement.

measurementDatetime.description: Date and time of the measurement.

DrugExposure.description: Represents a patient's drug exposure or medication.

drugConceptId.description: RxNorm / ATC code for the drug.

drugExposureStartDatetime.description: Start time of the drug exposure.

drugExposureEndDatetime.description: End time of the drug exposure.

doseUnitConceptId.description: Unit of measurement for the drug dose (mg, ml).

CareSite.title: CareSite
CareSite.description: Represents a hospital or clinic site.

careSiteId.description: Unique identifier for the CareSite entity.

providerId.description: Unique identifier for the Provider entity.

Location.title: Location
Location.description: Represents a physical location or address.

locationId.description: Unique identifier for the Location entity.

firestore.reasoning:
The Firestore structure is designed to provide a secure, scalable, and easily maintainable database for the MedVerseAI application, focusing on patient records and related healthcare data. It emphasizes authorization independence, clarity of intent, and adherence to the DBAC (Database Authentication and Control) principle.

Authorization Independence is achieved through structural segregation, where data with different access needs are stored in separate collections. Patient-specific data is nested under `/users/{userId}`, ensuring that access control is based on the authenticated user's ID. No `get()` calls are needed in the security rules to access parent data, enabling atomic operations and simplifying debugging.

The structure also adheres to QAPs (Rules are not Filters). The hierarchical structure under `/users/{userId}` ensures that listing operations can be securely performed based on the user's ID without requiring filtering. The separation of data types (Patient, Encounters, Conditions, etc.) into distinct collections further simplifies security rules and prevents unintended data exposure.

Specifically:

*   **Patients:** Patient data is stored under `/users/{userId}/patients/{patientId}`, establishing clear ownership and enabling secure retrieval of patient records. Each doctor or hospital staff member will have their own user id. Patient data will be stored according to the corresponding user id.
*   **Encounters, Conditions, Observations, Measurements, and DrugExposures:** These entities are stored as subcollections under `/users/{userId}/patients/{patientId}`, reflecting the 1:N relationship between patients and these entities. This structure ensures that access to these records is restricted to authorized users (doctors and hospital staff) who have access to the patient record.
*   **CareSites, Providers and Locations:** These are stored as top level collections and contain no PHI, therefore it's okay if they are globally readable.

This structure enables secure list operations since all reads are performed under `/users/{userId}` or public top-level collections such as care_sites, providers and locations.
